blocks.prompt: The House You Cut Out of the Ground
blocks.text: Iglu is a word from Inuktitut, the language of the Inuit. It just means house. Inuit hunters in the Arctic learned to build a house out of snow when they were far from home. First they find snow that the wind has packed hard. Then they cut it into blocks with a long knife. They set the blocks in a circle, then lay more blocks on top in a slow spiral. Each block leans on the one before it. The wall curves in and closes at the top. Last of all, the builder cuts a door and crawls out.

blocks.prompt: The House You Build From the Inside
blocks.text: When an Inuit hunter needs shelter on the sea ice, he does not look for wood. There are no trees. He looks for the right snow. Fresh snow is too soft. The snow he wants has been packed hard by wind, so hard that a block of it will hold your weight. He cuts the blocks with a pana, a long snow knife. Then he does something clever. He lays the first ring of blocks in a circle around himself, so he is standing inside his own house before it has walls. Instead of stacking neat rings, he cuts a ramp and builds upward in one long spiral. Every block leans against the block before it, so nothing can fall inward. At the top there is one last gap. He shapes a block, lifts it through the hole, and trims it until it drops in and locks the dome shut. Only then does he cut a door and crawl out into the wind. A good builder can do all of this in about an hour.

notes: Wind packed snow is mostly trapped air
Air is a poor conductor of heat

blocks.prompt: Why a House of Snow Is Warm
blocks.text: It sounds like a riddle. How can a house built out of frozen water keep a person warm? The answer is that snow is barely water at all. A block of wind packed snow is mostly air, trapped in millions of tiny pockets between the ice crystals. Air is a poor conductor of heat, which means heat moves through it slowly. Wool works the same way. So does the foam in a cooler. Snow is not warm. Snow is simply very good at refusing to let warmth leave. Inside an igloo, that trapped heat has somewhere to come from: the bodies of the people, and often a qulliq, a shallow lamp that burns seal oil with a wick of moss. Body heat alone can lift the air inside close to freezing while the wind outside sits at forty below. Add the lamp and the space near the roof can climb to shirtsleeve warmth. The design does the rest. The entrance tunnel is dug lower than the floor, so the cold, heavy air slides down into it and stays there instead of pooling around the sleepers. The sleeping platform is built high, because warm air rises. A small hole near the top of the dome lets stale air escape. And as the inside surface warms slightly, it melts and refreezes into a thin glaze of ice, which locks the whole dome together and makes it stronger, not weaker.

answers: a snow block is mostly air trapped in tiny pockets, not solid water
(inference: all three trap air, and trapped air slows heat down, so they insulate the same way)

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Snow is strong squeezed, weak bent
A dome puts every block in compression

Igloos were travel shelters, not year round homes

blocks.prompt: The Dome That Holds Itself Up
blocks.text: Ask most people to draw an igloo and you get a dome. Ask them why it is a dome and the answers run out. The shape is not decoration. It is the engineering. Snow is strong in one direction only. Squeeze it and it holds. Pull it or bend it and it crumbles. So a snow building has to be shaped so that every part of it is being squeezed. A dome does exactly that. Weight from the top presses down and outward along the curve, and each block passes the load to its neighbors until the whole thing arrives at the ground as pure compression. Nothing is hanging. Nothing is bending. Builders do not calculate this on paper. They inherited the correct curve through generations of building, failing, and adjusting, and the profile they settle on is close to the shape an engineer would arrive at with a formula. The construction method is just as deliberate. A builder does not lay stacked rings, which would leave every block unsupported until the ring closed. He cuts a ramp into the first course and spirals upward, so each block rests against the finished one behind it and cannot fall inward. He works from inside the growing dome, sealed in, until only a gap at the crown remains. The final block, the key, is passed up through that gap and shaved from below until it wedges tight. Then he cuts his own way out. There is a story people tell wrong. Igloos were not the year round homes of the Inuit. They were mostly built on the trail, by hunters far from camp, put up in an hour and abandoned in the morning. Families lived in sod and whalebone houses through the darkest months and in skin tents through the summer. The igloo was a travel shelter, which is exactly what makes it remarkable: a warm, windproof, structurally sound building assembled in an hour from the only material available, using one knife, and left behind without a trace when it melted.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Wind packed Arctic snow is roughly two thirds air by volume
Snow has compressive strength and almost no tensile strength
The profile is closer to a catenary than a hemisphere
Spiral courses let every block lean on a finished neighbor
The cold trap entrance sits below the sleeping floor
Igloos were trail shelters, raised in an hour and abandoned

blocks.prompt: One Knife, One Hour, Forty Below
blocks.text: Consider the problem. You are on the sea ice north of the Arctic Circle. The temperature is forty below and the wind has been rising for an hour. There is no wood, no stone you can reach, no soil, and nothing you did not carry in. Night is coming and it will last a very long time. You have one knife. Build a house. The Inuit answer to that problem is an engineering achievement that usually gets patronized as a curiosity. It begins with material science. Snow here is not the enemy, it is the insulation. Wind packed Arctic snow is roughly two thirds air by volume, held in millions of pockets between bonded ice crystals, and air conducts heat poorly. The snow does not warm anyone. It simply refuses to let warmth leave, which is all any insulation has ever done. The builder is not merely making do with the material at hand. He is using the cold's own product against it. Next comes structure. Snow has real compressive strength and almost no tensile strength: press it and it holds, stretch or bend it and it fails. A building made of snow must therefore be shaped so that no part of it is ever in tension. The dome does this. Load from the crown travels down the curve, block passing it to block, and reaches the ground as compression the whole way. The profile Inuit builders use is not a hemisphere. It is closer to a catenary, the curve a hanging chain makes, turned upside down, which is the shape engineers choose when they want an arch to carry its own weight with nothing pulling apart. Nobody derived it here. It was arrived at through generations of building, watching, and correcting, and it is correct. Then the assembly. Stacked rings would be a disaster, because every block in an unfinished ring has nothing to lean on. So the builder cuts a ramp into the first course and rises in a continuous spiral, each block braced by the one laid before it. He works from inside, walling himself in, which lets him trim every joint from the side that matters. The last gap at the crown takes the key block, lifted through and shaved from below until it jams. Only then does he cut a doorway and leave. The interior is managed with equal care. The entrance passage sits below the floor, so dense cold air pours into it and stays, a trap the warm air never has to fight. The sleeping platform is raised, because heat rises to meet it. A vent hole at the crown carries off stale air and moisture. Body heat and a qulliq, a seal oil lamp with a moss wick, can bring the upper air to shirtsleeve temperature while the wind outside strips heat from anything it touches. The inner surface melts a little and refreezes into a glaze of ice, and the dome gets stronger overnight. One correction is owed. Igloos were not, for most Inuit, permanent homes. They were built on the trail and left in the morning. Families wintered in sod and whalebone houses and summered in skin tents. That fact makes the igloo more impressive rather than less. This is disposable architecture: a warm, silent, structurally sound building raised in about an hour from a material that falls out of the sky for free, and returned to water in the spring without leaving anything behind at all.
